title: Spiritual ecumenism
hook: Vatican II calls prayer the soul of Christian unity

segments.voice: Yesterday, canon law, and its last line: the salvation of souls is the supreme law. Your line was for souls. Did a rule cross your path, and did you ask who it was for? Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

On the night before he died, Jesus prayed out loud for the people who would come after his friends, people he would never meet. John's Gospel keeps the words. He didn't ask that they be clever, or successful, or even safe. He asked that they be one. Christians have argued, split and sometimes fought ever since. And when the Catholic Church sat down at the Second Vatican Council to ask how to mend those splits, it put something before the meetings and the documents. Today, spiritual ecumenism.
screen: `THE NIGHT BEFORE HE DIED.` → `HE ASKED THAT THEY BE ONE.` → `SOMETHING BEFORE THE MEETINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the prayer itself. In the Douay-Rheims, John chapter seventeen: "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee; that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that thou hast sent me." Notice the last clause. Unity isn't only about Christians getting along. It's tied to whether the world can believe at all. Second, the word ecumenism. It's the work of Christians from divided churches seeking the unity Jesus prayed for. It includes theologians in dialogue and joint statements, and you'll meet some of those in the coming days. Third, what the council put first. The council's decree on ecumenism says that a change of heart and holiness of life, together with public and private prayer for the unity of Christians, should be seen as the soul of the whole ecumenical movement. And it gives this a name: spiritual ecumenism. The soul, the decree says. Not decoration on top of the real work, but what makes the work alive. Fourth, what that looks like. The same decree says Catholics may, in certain circumstances, join in prayer with other Christians for unity. There's even a week of prayer for Christian unity, when churches that can't yet share one altar still share one prayer. In the council's picture, changed hearts are the soul of the work, and the documents serve them. A dialogue between people who have prayed together starts from a different place than a negotiation between strangers.
screen: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · `CHRISTIANS SEEKING UNITY.` · `PRAYER IS THE SOUL OF IT.` · `HEARTS FIRST, THEN DOCUMENTS.` · then, large: `THAT THE WORLD MAY BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one Christian you know from a different church: a Baptist neighbor, an Orthodox coworker, a cousin who goes to a church with a band. Hold their face for a moment. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for unity, using the words of John seventeen: that they all may be one. If you don't pray, hold them in mind with goodwill. The fuller invitation is for later: if the chance comes, pray alongside another Christian, even just an Our Father said together. The bell holds the time.
Spiritual ecumenism. Change of heart, holiness of life and prayer for unity, which the council called the soul of the ecumenical movement. Today's word.
Your line: prayer first. Today, before you argue with someone, even in your head, pause long enough to wish them well. Day one thousand four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for Christian unity at Mass and in private, and join other Christians in shared services of prayer, especially during the week of prayer for Christian unity.

notes: Editor pass: 'the council's order is clear: hearts change first, then documents' overstated the decree, which calls change of heart and prayer the soul of the movement; reworded to match.

Unitatis Redintegratio 8 paraphrased: change of heart and holiness of life, along with public and private prayer for the unity of Christians, should be regarded as the soul of the whole ecumenical movement, and merit the name 'spiritual ecumenism'; in certain special circumstances it is allowable, indeed desirable, that Catholics join in prayer with separated brethren. Confirm.
Hook: Jesus praying for those who would believe through the disciples' word (John 17:20) 'on the night before he died' follows John's setting at the Last Supper; confirm framing.

'Christians have argued, split and sometimes fought ever since': a general historical statement; Keeper may soften.
